el-capitan.story: Traveller, in Yosemite National Park, on the north side of Yosemite Valley near its western end, you will find El Capitan, a vertical rock formation and granite monolith about 3,000 feet from base to summit along its tallest face. Its top can be reached by hiking out of Yosemite Valley on the trail next to Yosemite Falls, then proceeding west, while for climbers the challenge is to climb up the sheer granite face. Many named climbing routes, all of them arduous, include Iron Hawk and Sea of Dreams, and the formation is a world-famous location for big wall climbing, including aid climbing, free climbing, and more recently free solo climbing. The Mariposa Battalion named it El Capitán when they explored the valley in 1851, taking “the captain” as a loose Spanish translation of the local Miwok name Tutokanula, meaning “rock chief.”
el-capitan.name: El Capitan

yosemite-national-park.story: Welcome, traveller, to Yosemite National Park in California, bordered by Sierra National Forest to the southeast and Stanislaus National Forest to the northwest. Here you can find granite cliffs, waterfalls, clear streams, groves of giant sequoia, lakes, mountains, meadows, glaciers, and biological diversity, with almost 95 percent of the park designated wilderness. Managed by the National Park Service, this World Heritage Site was shaped by uplifted and tilted Sierra Nevada slopes, deep narrow canyons, and glaciers that cut and sculpted the U-shaped Yosemite Valley. Though about four million visitors come annually and most spend their time in the valley’s seven square miles, the park remains one of the largest and least fragmented habitat blocks in the Sierra Nevada.
yosemite-national-park.name: Yosemite National Park

half-dome.story: As you stand in Yosemite Valley, Half Dome rises at the eastern end, a quartz monzonite batholith named for its distinct shape: one sheer face while the other three sides are smooth and round, making it appear like a dome cut in half. It stands at over 8,800 feet above sea level, and at its core are the remains of a magma chamber that cooled slowly and crystallized beneath the Earth’s surface before erosion exposed and cut it in half. From the valley floor it seems like a round dome that has lost its northwest half, but from Washburn Point it can be seen as a thin ridge of rock, an arête, with its southeast side almost as steep as its northwest side except for the very top. As late as the 1870s it was described as “perfectly inaccessible” by Josiah Whitney, until George Anderson reached the summit in October 1875 via a route constructed by drilling and placing iron eye bolts, later adding ropes so other people could climb.
half-dome.name: Half Dome

mount-watkins-california.story: For a traveller in the Sierra Nevada, Mount Watkins is an 8,497-foot summit in Yosemite National Park, in Mariposa County, California, 2.72 miles north of Half Dome and 1.86 miles northwest of Clouds Rest. Its precipitation runoff drains into Tenaya Creek, a tributary of the Merced River, and the summit rises 2,700 feet above Tenaya Canyon in less than one mile. An ascent of the summit is 7.4 miles round-trip with 750 feet of elevation gain, with June through October offering the best conditions, approached via the Snow Creek Trail starting near Olmsted Point. Named after photographer Carleton Watkins, whose Yosemite photographs influenced Congress to preserve it as a National Park, the mountain also has the Native American name “Waijau,” meaning Pine Mountain.
mount-watkins-california.name: Mount Watkins (California)

sentinel-dome.story: Traveller, let Sentinel Dome be your granite perch in Yosemite National Park, United States, lying on the south wall of Yosemite Valley. From the top, a 360 degree view opens over Yosemite Valley and surroundings, where you can see Half Dome, El Capitan, Yosemite Falls, North Dome, Basket Dome, and much more, and at night it and nearby Glacier Point are popular places for stargazing under a 360 degree view of the night sky. The trail to the base is a relatively easy 1.1-mile hike from the same trailhead as Taft Point, located 6 miles from Bridalveil Creek on the Glacier Point road, and once at the base hikers traverse the less imposing northeast granite slope to the summit. In winter, you can reach Sentinel Dome from Badger Pass by a 10-miles ski tour.
sentinel-dome.name: Sentinel Dome

tenaya-lake.story: At Tenaya Lake, an alpine lake in Yosemite National Park between Yosemite Valley and Tuolumne Meadows, the surface has an elevation of 8,150 feet. Its basin was formed by glacial action, leaving a backdrop of light granite rocks whose beauty was known to the Native Americans, and today it is easily accessible by State Route 120 and popular for water activities. The lake is named after Chief Tenaya, chief of the native people who lived in Yosemite Valley before being driven out by the Mariposa Battalion; when told the lake was named in his honor, he pointed at the glistening peaks near the head of the lake and said it already had a name, Py-we-ack. That original name is now attached to Pywiack Dome, a granite dome to the east, while the area became the first park land federally protected for preservation and public use as part of the 1864 Yosemite grant, and John Muir wrote of the lake’s beauty and timelessness in 1868.
tenaya-lake.name: Tenaya Lake

cathedral-peak-california.story: Traveller, let Cathedral Peak welcome you as part of the Cathedral Range, a mountain range in the south-central portion of Yosemite National Park in eastern Mariposa and Tuolumne Counties, an offshoot of the Sierra Nevada. Its cathedral-shaped peak was formed by glacial activity, remaining uneroded above the glaciers in the Pleistocene, and to the west is Eichorn Pinnacle, named for Jules Eichorn, who first ascended a class 5.4 route to its summit on July 24, 1931, with Glen Dawson. In 1869, John Muir wrote in My first summer in the Sierra that the body of the Cathedral is nearly square, its roof slopes wonderfully regular and symmetrical, its ridge trending northeast and southwest, with a magnificent northeast gable, a big snow-bank at its base, and a front adorned with many pinnacles and a tall spire. Muir also noted the Cathedral is said to be about eleven thousand feet above the sea, about fifteen hundred feet above the ridge it stands on, and a mile or so westward a handsome lake shines with glacier-polished granite, making the line between rock and water not easy to trace.
cathedral-peak-california.name: Cathedral Peak (California)

mount-clark-california.story: As you travel toward Mount Clark, you’re approaching an 11,527-foot granite peak in the Clark Range, a sub-range of the Sierra Nevada and a popular destination for mountaineers. Both the mountain and the range are named in honor of Galen Clark, an early explorer and the first guardian of Yosemite National Park; before its present name, it was known as Gothic Peak and then The Obelisk, the name used by the Whitney Survey. It was summited in 1866 by Clarence King and James Gardener of the US Geological Survey, and Obelisk Lake, at 9,853 feet, lies on the mountain’s northeast flank. In this alpine climate zone, most weather fronts originate in the Pacific Ocean and travel east toward the Sierra Nevada, where the peaks force them upward and cause them to drop moisture as rain or snowfall onto the range.
mount-clark-california.name: Mount Clark (California)
